name: MyPowerbox - Mobile app MV
headline: Launched the first official Mobilize mobile app around a connected charging product, turning hardware constraints into a usable daily experience.
roleSummary: Owned the UI direction and drove the UX flows end-to-end, from prototyping through brand alignment and user testing.
summary: Defined the visual language, interaction patterns, and screen architecture for Mobilize's first connected charging product. The resulting design system became the foundation for the brand's mobile experiences.
challenge: Designing one of the first official Mobilize mobile experiences meant turning a technically constrained charging-station product into a clear day-to-day app, while shaping an emerging brand with limited budget and white-label ambitions.

blocks.content: Designing the first official Mobilize mobile app around a physical home-charging product meant turning hardware constraints, pairing friction, and a young brand into a usable daily experience that could scale over time.

items.label: Scope
items.value:
UI / UX Designer with UI ownership and UX co-construction

Responsibilities

UI design, prototype creation, brand collaboration, user testing, mobile design-system foundations, Lottie and Rive motion work

items.label: Team and setup
items.value:
UX Designer, Product Leader, Product Owner, 2 Developers, Renault Energy Design studio, Brand Vision team

Tools

Figma and FigJam, Jira, Rive, Lottie, Teams

Timeline

2023

blocks.title: Key points
items: Create a credible first Mobilize mobile experience around the MyPowerbox charging station
Design a navigation model built for daily use, not only initial setup
Support white-label B2B potential while delivering a strong B2C product
Establish early mobile design-system foundations for the Mobilize ecosystem

blocks.content: The project carried four overlapping product risks.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Value risk: the app was tied to a physical charging station with limited differentiation in a crowded EV market. The experience had to make the product feel useful beyond first setup.

Usability risk: pairing a physical device to a mobile app created strong technical constraints. Half of test users struggled to navigate parameters, and the charging wheel was misread as a call to action.
Viability risk: Mobilize was a young brand with no established mobile identity. The app had to feel credible as a consumer product while staying flexible for future enterprise white-label deployment.
Feasibility risk: limited budget, SAFe constraints, and a physical-device dependency meant the design had to work inside tight boundaries.

blocks.content: I was the principal owner of the UI work, with strong involvement in product shaping.
My contribution included:

blocks.title: Key points
items: designing the full MVP interface from home dashboard to charging management, settings, and edge cases
co-constructing UX decisions with the UX Designer through co-design workshops
creating a complete interactive prototype with motion for validation and development
defining and running a guerrilla test covering first impressions, pairing flow smoothness, and secondary-feature usability
collaborating with Renault Energy Design studio and Brand Vision team on the first Mobilize visual direction
building the first mobile design-system components for the Mobilize ecosystem
running acceptance testing to verify component behavior and appearance after development
setting up HEART metrics to measure user experience and engagement

blocks.title: Research evidence
blocks.description: Show the competitive benchmark board with key user flows, positive patterns, and weak points across competitors.
blocks.caption: Wireframes and initial flows

blocks.title: What I learned from the current product

blocks.content: The guerrilla test on the MVP prototype revealed six concrete usability problems:

blocks.title: Key points
items: Half of users could not navigate through parameters
Security settings were hard to find in the list
Users had difficulty passing forms when the button was below the fold
The solution lacked enough guidance
Users interpreted the charging wheel as a call to action
UX writing was imprecise in several flows

blocks.content: The pairing flow was the most sensitive area. Because the experience depended on a physical product, technical constraints heavily shaped the UX and required multiple iterations with product and technical stakeholders.

blocks.title: Test findings board
blocks.description: Show the 6 usability issues with severity, screenshots, and the fixes they triggered.
blocks.caption: Brainwriting workshop — ideation session

blocks.content: The original app structure was setup-centric. I restructured navigation around recurring daily actions: checking charging status, managing sessions, and accessing settings. Testing confirmed users needed clearer navigation landmarks, which led to adding a bottom tab bar.

blocks.title: A clearer pairing flow with stronger guidance

blocks.content: The pairing flow between the charging station and the app was the highest-friction area. I iterated it multiple times with architects and the Product Leader to reduce unnecessary steps and clarify system feedback.

blocks.title: Pairing flow feedback
blocks.description: Show one short sequence with state changes, loading feedback, and success confirmation.
blocks.caption: Redesigned pairing flow

blocks.title: Lottie and Rive animations for product credibility

blocks.content: I crafted animations in Figma, then reconstructed them with Lottie and Rive so developers could integrate them more easily. These motion details helped the app feel polished and credible as a first Mobilize product, not only a functional utility.

Design decisions were grounded in two validated personae: the Early adopter who wanted visibility over all connected devices, and the Gradual discovery user who wanted simplified energy management. This kept the product tied to real behavior differences rather than generic assumptions.

blocks.title: An early Mobilize mobile design system

blocks.content: I built the first component library for Mobilize mobile apps and documented behavior through interactive prototypes. This created a reusable base that extended beyond MyPowerbox to other Mobilize products.

blocks.title: System foundations
blocks.description: Show the early Mobilize mobile library with key components, states, and usage patterns.
blocks.caption: MVP result

blocks.content: The MVP launched on iOS and Android app stores and was validated through testing.
Beyond the release:

blocks.title: Key points
items: the concept was reused as a foundation for V2 of the product
the mobile design-system layer became a shared base for future Mobilize apps
V2 explorations opened a broader MyEnergy platform direction connecting charging to a wider energy ecosystem

blocks.quote: The project did not only ship as an MVP. It created a reusable base for later iterations, brand maturation, and future product extensions.

blocks.title: Research, workshops, and exploration details
blocks.content:
RESEARCH AND EXPLORATION DETAILS

The project followed a full double-diamond approach: Discover, Define, Develop, Deploy.

Key activities included:

- alignment workshops with key stakeholders to clarify business goals

- problem framing around EV charging positioning in a crowded market

- interview synthesis during exploration

- competitive benchmark mapping flows and positive or negative patterns across competitors

- brainwriting workshops with potential users

- two validated personae: Early adopter and Gradual discovery

- user-journey mapping to identify IoT-specific friction points

- HEART metrics setup

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original workshop boards, competitive analysis, and journey artifacts are preserved in the archived case study here:

MyPowerbox archive with original process visuals

blocks.title: Pairing flow, testing, and iteration details
blocks.content:
PAIRING FLOW, TESTING, AND ITERATION DETAILS

The pairing flow required synchronization with architects and the Product Leader across multiple iterations. Critical technical constraints were collected during the definition phase.

The guerrilla test covered three objectives:

1. check user impressions and understanding on first use

1. observe the smoothness of the pairing process

1. examine understanding and usability of secondary features

Post-test, we reworked the information hierarchy through a workshop and added a bottom tab bar to simplify navigation.

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original pairing-flow wireframes, handoff flow, and test outputs are preserved in the archived case study here:

MyPowerbox archive with original process visuals

blocks.title: Design system and delivery details
blocks.content:
DESIGN SYSTEM AND DELIVERY DETAILS

I built the first mobile component library for Mobilize products and documented behavior through interactive prototypes.

During handoff, I created complete user flows capturing interdependencies with other features and edge cases. Detailed functional specifications accompanied each flow.

Acceptance testing verified component behavior and appearance after development, with priority-based correction tracking.

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original design-system captures are preserved in the archived case study here:

MyPowerbox archive with original process visuals

This project taught me how different mobile design becomes when the product is tied to a physical device. The UX is not only about screens, but about helping people succeed through technical uncertainty.

It also showed how much responsibility sits inside a first product for a young brand. The interface becomes part of the brand definition itself. If I were to redo this, I would map brand-governance stakeholders earlier and invest more in framing workshops before diving into detailed design.

name: FleetUI - Web App Design
headline: Turned a fragmented fleet tool into a credible B2B dashboard platform for administrators and managers.
roleSummary: Redesigned existing screens and created new product views. Defined the framing logic and reusable dashboard patterns that structured the platform.
summary: Designed the UX and UI foundations of FleetUI, restructuring disconnected workflows into a coherent dashboard platform for fleet administrators and managers.
challenge: Turning an internal, fragmented fleet tool into a credible B2B platform required making complex telematics data easier to navigate and act on, despite no strong UX foundation and multiple disconnected workflows.

blocks.content: Transforming a fragmented internal fleet tool into a credible B2B SaaS dashboard platform meant making dense telematics data easier to navigate, easier to act on, and easier to trust for administrators and fleet managers.

items.label: Scope
items.value:
UI / UX Designer

Responsibilities

Screen redesign, new feature design, research and framing, reusable dashboard patterns, product design-system layer, developer collaboration

items.label: Team and setup
items.value:
UX Designer, Product Manager, 2 Product Owners, 2 Developers, Mobilize Financial Services

Tools

Figma and FigJam, Jira, Teams

Timeline

2023 to 2024

blocks.title: Key points
items: Make fleet data easier to navigate and act on for operational users
Move the product from internal-tool logic toward a credible B2B platform
Create reusable dashboard patterns instead of solving each screen in isolation
Reduce cognitive overload in a data-heavy environment

blocks.title: Main dashboard hierarchy
blocks.intro: Compare the original scattered dashboard with the redesigned task-oriented structure. Add 2 images later with captions Before and After.
blocks.beforeBody: Legacy before visual or initial state

blocks.content: The product carried four overlapping risks.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Value risk: the existing tool was built for internal operators, not external fleet managers. Their needs, mental models, and expectations were fundamentally different.
Usability risk: fleet data was spread across disconnected tools with no coherent navigation. Key information existed but was not presented in a way that supported action.
Viability risk: the product needed to become credible enough to sell as a B2B SaaS in a highly competitive market where players like Geotab and Samsara already had mature UX.
Feasibility risk: the product had to scale across multiple user profiles and task types without becoming harder to navigate.

blocks.content: I identified the need for this product after learning that existing tools for fleet managers within Renault were either costly external platforms or internal products built without UX consideration.
My contribution included:

blocks.title: Key points
items: conducting stakeholder interviews and market research to understand the fleet-management ecosystem
running a heuristic evaluation of the existing interface to map structural UX problems
performing competitive analysis against established players in the fleet-management space
conducting user interviews with fleet administrators and managers
redesigning existing screens to improve usability and readability
designing new product views including fleet dashboards, asset detail pages, event tracking, and map interfaces
creating reusable dashboard patterns and layout templates for systematic feature development
building a dedicated design-system layer for the dashboard product
collaborating with developers on component logic and implementation alignment

blocks.title: Research and audit evidence
blocks.description: Show the heuristic evaluation board with fragmented navigation, weak hierarchy, and inconsistent component behavior highlighted.
blocks.caption: Asset details screen

blocks.title: What I learned from the current product

blocks.content: The heuristic evaluation and user research revealed recurring structural problems:

blocks.title: Key points
items: navigation between fleet-level and asset-level views was unclear and inconsistent
data tables lacked strong hierarchy, making it difficult to separate critical information from noise
the interface mixed operational views and administrative views without clear separation
there was no coherent visual system connecting dashboard components across screens
users had to context-switch between multiple tools to complete basic fleet-management tasks

blocks.content: The product was not broken screen by screen. The problem was systemic: no coherent structure connected the screens into a usable platform.

blocks.title: Benchmark comparison
blocks.description: Show how competitors structure navigation, data density, filters, and table readability across 3 to 5 fleet platforms.
blocks.caption: Events log — existing product state

blocks.content: I restructured navigation so it matched real operational workflows rather than exposing data by source. Fleet view, asset view, tables, maps, and event tracking became connected views supporting the way administrators actually monitor and manage vehicles.

Rather than treating each screen as a separate design problem, I built a pattern library of dashboard components: data cards, status indicators, table configurations, and chart layouts. This created coherence across screens and made future feature design more systematic.

blocks.title: Reduced cognitive load on data-heavy screens

blocks.content: I redesigned the information hierarchy on tables and maps so fleet managers could scan, filter, and act without being overwhelmed. This included clearer visual weight, better progressive disclosure, and smarter default views.

I created a product-specific design-system base that extended the general component library with dashboard-specific patterns such as data-visualization components, status badges, KPI cards, and responsive table behaviors.

Research and workshops helped the team move from isolated feature thinking toward a coherent platform direction. I contributed to defining three core product values: availability, reliability, and comfort of management.

blocks.title: Dashboard pattern set
blocks.description: Show data cards, KPI layout, status badges, table configuration, and event monitoring patterns side by side.
blocks.caption: Fleet map view

blocks.content: The project helped transform a fragmented internal starting point into a more coherent B2B dashboard foundation.
Key results:

blocks.title: Key points
items: improved usability around core fleet-management tasks through clearer navigation and data hierarchy
established a scalable dashboard pattern library that made future feature design more systematic
contributed to a stronger product vision through research, workshops, and competitive positioning
created a design-system layer that gave the product a more consistent and professional visual identity

blocks.quote: The strongest shift was structural. The product moved from disconnected tooling logic toward a more readable, task-oriented platform foundation that could support future growth.

blocks.title: Research, audit, and workshop details
blocks.content:
RESEARCH, AUDIT, AND WORKSHOP DETAILS

The project included stakeholder interviews, market research, heuristic evaluation, competitive analysis, and user interviews.

These inputs helped reveal both the business opportunity and the structural UX problems of the existing tools, including fragmented workflows, weak navigation, and underused data potential.

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original heuristic audit, benchmark boards, and interview artifacts are preserved in the archived case study here:

FleetUI archive with original process visuals

blocks.title: Design system, templates, and delivery details
blocks.content:
DESIGN SYSTEM, TEMPLATES, AND DELIVERY DETAILS

Alongside the product work, I contributed to a dedicated design-system layer for the dashboard product.

This included reusable components, layout logic, templates, and collaboration practices with developers so the product could evolve on a more stable UI foundation.

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original framing artifacts, wireframes, and handoff batches are preserved in the archived case study here:

FleetUI archive with original process visuals

This project reinforced how much B2B dashboard design depends on task clarity, not only information density. When users manage operations at scale, navigation and structure matter as much as visual polish.

It also taught me how valuable reusable patterns become when a product is still defining its long-term platform shape. Looking back, I would push for real user testing earlier to validate navigation assumptions, and involve developers sooner in the pattern library definition to prevent implementation gaps.

name: Citadel Team - Mobile & Web App
headline: Redesigned the videoconferencing experience across mobile and web, making call actions intuitive and layouts scalable from 1-to-1 to group calls.
roleSummary: Solo product designer responsible for the full videoconferencing redesign, from audit through delivery, while chat was the established default surface.
summary: Redesigned Citadel Team's video conferencing experience across mobile and web, rethinking the action hierarchy and layout system to scale cleanly as participant counts changed.
challenge: The original video conferencing experience was difficult to scale as participant counts changed, while key UI actions and icons were not always intuitive across mobile and web.

blocks.content: Redesigning Citadel Team's video conferencing experience across mobile and web, solving action clarity and layout scalability problems that made the feature harder to use as participant counts increased.
Role
Product Designer (solo on conferencing scope)
Responsibilities
UX/UI design, interface affordance audit, icon clarity improvement, layout scalability, guerrilla testing, benchmark
Collaborators
Product Owner, CTO, Developers
Environment
Startup environment backed by Thales funds. Small, lean team with effectively solo design ownership on the conferencing scope.
Tools
Citadel Team, Figma, Zeplin, Jira
Timeline

blocks.title: Key points
items: Make core conferencing actions (mute, camera, share) immediately understandable without interpretation
Create a layout system that stays readable as participant counts scale from 2 to 10+
Improve the overall credibility of the conferencing feature as a real-time collaboration tool

blocks.title: Visual proof
blocks.description: Placeholder image — Add the scalable layout system showing how the conference grid adapts from 2 participants to 4, 6, and 10+ across desktop and mobile.
blocks.caption: Internal UX audit — issues identified

blocks.content: The conferencing feature sat at the intersection of two critical UX problems.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Action clarity risk: conference controls had to feel immediate and self-explanatory. In a real-time context, users cannot afford to pause and interpret an icon. The original interface had contrast and hierarchy issues, insufficient feedback on interactive elements, and weak differentiation between primary and secondary actions.

Layout scalability risk: the interface worked for small calls but degraded as participant counts increased. The layout logic did not adapt well across screen sizes and call configurations, creating visual clutter and reducing readability.

Product credibility risk: video conferencing was the standout new feature differentiating Citadel from pure messaging competitors. If the experience felt clunky, it undermined the product's positioning as a serious collaboration platform for security-conscious organizations.
Feasibility risk: lean team context with solo design ownership meant every decision had to count, with limited room for extensive exploration.

blocks.content: I was the sole designer on the conferencing scope, with the chat product already established as the core surface.
My contribution included:

blocks.title: Key points
items: auditing the existing conference experience to map contrast issues, hierarchy problems, and interaction weaknesses
benchmarking conferencing tools (Zoom, Teams, Google Meet) to identify best practices for action visibility, icon clarity, and participant layouts
running ideation work with stakeholders to explore more flexible interface structures
redesigning core conference controls for clearer affordance and faster recognition
creating a scalable layout system that adapted to different participant-count scenarios
conducting guerrilla testing on specific usability questions: mute recognition on desktop, icon clarity on mobile, layout readability with increasing participants
iterating based on test findings to confirm direction and reduce ambiguity

blocks.title: Visual proof
blocks.description: Placeholder image — Add a zoom on the improved conference controls: mute/unmute, camera, share screen, showing the icon redesign and visual feedback states.
blocks.caption: Ideation workshop (6-to-1 method)

blocks.title: What I learned from the current product

blocks.content: The audit and benchmark revealed specific weaknesses in the original interface:

blocks.title: Key points
items: contrast between active and inactive control states was insufficient for quick scanning
icon metaphors for some actions required interpretation rather than being immediately obvious
the hierarchy between primary actions (mute, camera) and secondary actions (settings, participants list) was too flat
the layout became visually cluttered beyond 4 participants, with no clear system to manage grid transitions
feedback on state changes (e.g., microphone muted) was not prominent enough for real-time awareness

blocks.content: These were not cosmetic issues. In a conferencing context, every fraction of a second spent interpreting controls is a UX failure.

blocks.title: Clearer action hierarchy with stronger affordance

blocks.content: I reworked the placement, sizing, and visual weight of core conference actions. Primary controls (mute, camera, end call) received more visual prominence. Secondary controls (settings, participant list) were visually separated to reduce cognitive load during active calls.

blocks.title: Redesigned icon system with explicit feedback states

blocks.content: I treated icon clarity as a core usability issue, not a cosmetic detail. Each control got explicit visual states: active, inactive, hover, and disabled. The mute icon specifically received attention after guerrilla testing confirmed users needed faster recognition on desktop.

I restructured the participant grid to handle transitions between different call sizes. The system defined clear layout rules for 1:1 calls, small groups (3-4), medium groups (5-8), and larger calls (9+). Each configuration had specific rules for tile sizing, speaker highlighting, and overflow behavior.

Mobile conferencing required different affordance rules than desktop. I adapted the control bar layout, icon sizes, and gesture interactions to work within mobile constraints while maintaining the same clarity principles.

blocks.title: Visual proof
blocks.description: Placeholder image — Add the guerrilla test findings: mute recognition results on desktop, icon clarity scores on mobile, layout readability feedback.
blocks.caption: Redesigned mobile video conference UI

blocks.content: The redesign gave the conference feature a stronger and more scalable UX foundation across mobile and web.
Key results:

blocks.title: Key points
items: improved clarity of core actions through better icon affordance and visual hierarchy
created a layout system resilient to participant-count variation, from 1:1 to 10+ users
validated key interaction choices through targeted guerrilla testing
the feature set was shipped and continued to evolve after my time on the product, confirming the redesign worked as a durable base rather than a one-off visual refresh

blocks.quote: The conferencing feature evolved from a functional add-on into a more credible real-time collaboration experience that could support the product's positioning against established competitors.

blocks.title: Research and exploration details
blocks.content:
RESEARCH AND EXPLORATION

I started by auditing the existing experience and benchmarking how other conferencing tools handled action visibility, icon clarity, and participant layouts.

This phase helped identify recurring weaknesses: contrast issues, insufficient feedback, weak action differentiation, and layouts that degraded under complexity.

I also ran ideation work with stakeholders to explore more flexible interface structures.

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original audit, benchmark, and ideation boards are preserved in the archived case study here:

Citadel conference archive with original process visuals

blocks.title: Testing and iteration details
blocks.content:
TESTING AND ITERATION

We ran guerrilla tests on specific usability questions instead of trying to validate everything at once.

The most useful checks focused on:

- whether users understood the mute action quickly on desktop

- whether the chosen icons felt clear enough on mobile

- whether the new layout logic made participant display easier to parse

This helped confirm the direction and reduce ambiguity around the most sensitive interaction choices.

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original mindmap and guerrilla-test artifacts are preserved in the archived case study here:

Citadel conference archive with original process visuals
This project taught me how much conferencing UX depends on interaction clarity under pressure. In real-time collaboration, action hierarchy and affordance matter as much as visual quality.

It also reinforced the importance of designing interface structures that can scale with product complexity instead of solving only the current state. In hindsight, I would invest more in systematic layout testing across participant-count scenarios, and advocate for a product-wide icon audit rather than scoping it only to conferencing.

name: Citadel Team - Design System implementation
headline: Built Thales Ercom's first design system to create a shared language between design and development.
roleSummary: Solo owner of the system: foundations, component library, documentation, governance, and collaboration rituals with engineering.
summary: Built Thales Ercom's first design system as a solo designer, establishing a shared vocabulary and component architecture that bridged design and development in a low-maturity, partly remote environment.
challenge: No shared design language or source of truth existed, creating inconsistencies, repeated QA, and friction between design and development when building components in a low-maturity, partly remote environment.

blocks.content: Building Thales Ercom's first design system as a solo designer, creating a shared language between design and development to reduce inconsistency, repeated QA, and collaboration friction in a low-maturity, partly remote environment.
Role
Product Designer (solo design-system owner)
Responsibilities
Foundations definition, Figma component library, ZeroHeight documentation, reusable templates, component tracking, developer collaboration rituals
Collaborators
Product Manager, UI Designer, Developers
Environment
Design studio context at Thales Ercom. Partly remote, low design-system maturity at the start.
Tools
Figma, ZeroHeight, Zeplin, Sketch (legacy), Citadel Team, Jira
Timeline

blocks.title: Key points
items: Create a single source of truth for design foundations and components
Establish a shared vocabulary between design and development
Reduce repeated QA loops caused by inconsistent component interpretation
Raise the team's design-system maturity from near-zero to a sustainable foundation

blocks.title: Visual proof
blocks.description: Placeholder image — Add a before/after comparison: inconsistent component implementations across screens vs. standardized components from the design system.
blocks.caption: DS audit and weekly definition sessions

blocks.content: The challenge was not purely visual. It was organizational.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Alignment risk: no shared source of truth meant design and development interpreted components differently. The same button could look and behave differently across screens, with no way to determine which version was correct.

Adoption risk: introducing a design system in a low-maturity environment meant the team had to learn new practices while continuing to ship product. If the system was too complex or not integrated into daily workflows, it would be ignored.

Documentation risk: a Figma library alone was not enough. Without clear usage rules, contribution guidelines, and behavior documentation, the system would become another set of files that slowly diverged from implementation.

Sustainability risk: as the sole designer building the system, I had to create something that could survive beyond my involvement. The system needed to be simple enough for others to maintain and extend.

blocks.content: I owned the initiative end-to-end on the design side.
My contribution included:

blocks.title: Key points
items: defining the foundation layer: color tokens, typography scale, spacing system, elevation rules
building a complete Figma component library with variants, states, and interaction rules
documenting every foundation and component in ZeroHeight with usage guidelines and implementation notes
creating reusable page templates so teams could start from coherent structures
setting up component tracking to monitor progress and alignment between design and implementation
establishing recurring follow-up rituals with Product and Tech to keep the system evolving
collaborating directly with developers on component creation logic and handoff clarity

blocks.title: Visual proof
blocks.description: Placeholder image — Add a ZeroHeight documentation sample showing a component page: visual specs, usage rules, states, and implementation notes.
blocks.caption: Component tracking sheet

blocks.title: What I learned from the existing state

blocks.content: The audit of the existing product revealed systematic inconsistency:

blocks.title: Key points
items: the same input component existed in 4 different visual variations across screens
button hierarchy was inconsistent: primary and secondary styles were used interchangeably
spacing was arbitrary, with no shared grid or spacing scale
color usage was based on individual judgment rather than shared tokens
developers had no reliable reference to check component behavior, leading to repeated QA cycles where design and development debated what was correct

blocks.content: The cost was not just visual inconsistency. It was time: every component handoff required explanation, every QA review required re-verification, and every new screen required re-discussion of decisions that should have been settled.

blocks.title: A foundation layer that removed guesswork

blocks.content: I defined color tokens, typography scale, spacing system, and elevation rules. These were not abstract design decisions. They were constraints that eliminated daily micro-decisions: which gray to use, how much spacing between elements, what shadow depth to apply.

blocks.title: A component library with clear variants and states

blocks.content: Each component in the Figma library included all its variants (size, type, state), with explicit naming conventions that matched the vocabulary developers used. This reduced the translation gap between design files and implementation.

blocks.title: ZeroHeight documentation as a collaboration tool

blocks.content: I documented every component not just with visual specs, but with usage guidelines: when to use this component vs. alternatives, what behaviors are expected, what accessibility considerations apply. The documentation served as a shared contract between design and development.

I created templates for recurring page types so the team could start from coherent structures. This prevented the drift that happens when every new page is built from scratch with individual interpretation of the system.

I established a tracking system to monitor which components were designed, documented, and implemented. Regular follow-up sessions with Product and Tech turned the system from a one-way handoff into a collaborative process.

blocks.title: Visual proof
blocks.description: Placeholder image — Add the component tracking board showing progress across designed, documented, and implemented statuses.
blocks.caption: ZeroHeight documentation

blocks.content: The project gave the team its first real design-system foundation and measurably improved collaboration.
Key results:

blocks.title: Key points
items: raised design and development maturity from near-zero to a structured shared practice
reduced repeated QA loops by giving developers a reliable source of truth
improved handoff clarity through documented component behavior and shared vocabulary
created a foundation that continued evolving after this first version, confirming it was sustainable
recommended adoption of Storybook to bridge the remaining gap between design documentation and live implementation

blocks.quote: The most important result was not a component library. It was a more shared language between design and development that reduced friction and made product work more predictable.

blocks.title: Process, tracking, and documentation details
blocks.content:
PROCESS AND DOCUMENTATION DETAILS

To make the system sustainable, I set up recurring follow-up rituals and tracking documents.

This included:

- component tracking to monitor progress and alignment

- reusable templates to standardize recurring work

- ZeroHeight documentation to centralize usage rules and component understanding

- regular discussions with Product and Tech to refine the system over time

These process elements mattered because the team was still building its design-system culture while the system itself was being created.

ARCHIVED PROCESS VISUALS

The original organization workshops, component tracking, and documentation captures are preserved in the archived case study here:

Citadel design-system archive with original process visuals

blocks.title: Constraints and team context
blocks.content:
CONSTRAINTS AND TEAM CONTEXT

The project had to move forward in a context with limited prior design-system maturity.

Main constraints included:

- low shared knowledge of design-system methods

- inconsistent alignment patterns between design and development

- a partly remote context that made informal synchronization less reliable

- the need to create structure while products were still evolving

- migration from Sketch to Figma happening in parallel
This project taught me that a design system is only partly a UI problem. It is also an alignment problem, a documentation problem, and a collaboration problem.

Building the first version of a system in a low-maturity environment forced me to think not only about components, but about adoption, language, and team habits. If I did it again, I would push for Storybook integration from the start and establish clearer contribution rules earlier to avoid the system depending on a single person.

name: Home Charging Quotation Tool
headline: Reduced uncertainty around home charging installation by turning a confusing EV buying step into a clear conversion path.
roleSummary: Principal UI designer responsible for the step-by-step journey design, interaction clarity, and cross-team alignment between product, business, and development.
summary: Designed the end-to-end home charging quotation experience for Renault and Dacia, reducing pricing uncertainty through a step-by-step journey embedded directly in the EV purchase ecosystem.
challenge: EV buyers faced pricing uncertainty around home charging installation, while Renault and Dacia websites did not make the offer easy enough to find or understand. Mobilize Power Solutions needed a more visible, more comprehensible, and more actionable experience.

blocks.content: Installing a home charging station is one of the biggest unknowns in the EV buying journey. On Renault and Dacia websites, users only saw a generic default price, with no way to understand how their own home setup could affect the final cost.

At the same time, competitors were already integrating estimation tools into their purchase journeys. Mobilize Power Solutions needed a quotation experience that could reduce uncertainty, support lead generation, and make the charging offer more visible inside the Renault ecosystem.

blocks.quote: I designed the home charging quotation experience to solve two linked problems: making the offer easier to find, and making the tool easier to understand.

blocks.caption: Home Charging Quotation Tool — embedded across Renault and Dacia configurators

blocks.content: This project had two UX challenges in sequence.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Discoverability: before users could use a quotation tool, they first had to find the charging offer in the existing content architecture.
Comprehension: once inside the flow, technical concepts and pricing logic made the experience harder to understand than it should have been.

blocks.content: An initial study made the discoverability issue clear: only 3 out of 18 participants found the relevant MPS page on renault.fr unaided.
Later prototype testing revealed the second issue: users were blocked by technical concepts such as monophasé, triphasé, and bidirectional charging, while the price logic felt too opaque.

blocks.caption: Existing experience — home charging buried, no estimation, no guidance

blocks.content: My main contribution was not to invent the whole product from scratch, but to make it clearer, more contemporary, more usable, and more deliverable.
I worked especially on:

blocks.title: Key points
items: refining and modernizing the UI
improving affordance and overall market fit of the experience
simplifying a potentially complex selection journey as much as possible
preparing a more elaborate handoff
collaborating with developers and stakeholders to resolve technical constraints
helping surface the right legal information in the right places
supporting a partner-routing logic so users could be redirected toward the most relevant next step

blocks.title: Key points
items: Value risk: helped validate whether users would engage with a home charging estimation offer inside the EV journey, and which entry points created real intent
Usability risk: simplified technical concepts, clarified price logic, and made the journey easier to follow step by step
Viability risk: aligned the experience with lead-generation goals and with Mobilize Power Solutions' visibility inside Renault's ecosystem
Feasibility risk: shaped a progressive flow that could be delivered responsively and later extended to additional cases such as co-ownership

blocks.content: Instead of treating the project as a single UI problem, I framed it as two consecutive challenges: first make the offer findable, then make the quotation flow understandable.

blocks.caption: Two-step flow — technical eligibility check before product selection

blocks.content: A major part of the redesign focused on reducing confusion around charging concepts. I introduced more contextual help and clearer educational moments so users could keep moving without needing expert knowledge.

The selection journey was simplified as much as possible so users could answer potentially complex questions without feeling like they were filling out a technical form. The ambition was closer to a guided purchase flow than to a heavy questionnaire.

blocks.title: Product selection: before and after
blocks.intro: The original selection flow asked users to understand technical specs before choosing a product. The redesign reversed that logic — context first, product second.
blocks.beforeBody: Original product selection UI — spec-first, no guidance

blocks.content: I reworked how pricing reacted to configuration choices so users could better understand why the estimate changed and what was influencing the result.
Part of the value of the tool also came from how it could redirect users toward the right partners and continuation paths, instead of leaving them with a price and no useful follow-up.

The experience was designed for both desktop and mobile, with mobile receiving special attention because of the traffic context and the need to reduce cognitive load on smaller screens. I also worked on a more robust handoff and closer collaboration with development and stakeholders to make the flow implementable under real technical and legal constraints.

blocks.caption: Responsive design — desktop and mobile layouts delivered to dev

blocks.content: End-to-end quotation tool shipped and embedded across Renault and Dacia EV purchase journeys.

blocks.title: First 6 weeks after launch
blocks.intro: The tool launched in September 2025 and quickly validated the strategy behind the experience.

items.label: Traffic from the 3 targeted entry points

blocks.content: These results matter because they validate more than just conversion. They show that embedding the quotation experience directly at the point of intent was the right move.

blocks.caption: Delivered tool — live on Renault and Dacia configurator pages

blocks.quote: The tool worked both as a lead engine and as a price-discovery experience. Even when users did not convert, the product still solved a major anxiety point in the EV journey.
The strongest signal was not only the number of leads generated, but the confirmation that users were entering the tool from the exact pages where charging intent was highest.

blocks.title: Research and testing details
blocks.content:
RESEARCH AND TESTING DETAILS

The project included an initial qualitative study with 18 participants focused on discoverability, followed by a second test cycle with 14 participants on the quotation prototype.

The most important insights were:

- users struggled to find the charging offer in the existing site structure

- monophasé / triphasé created the biggest comprehension barrier

- product comparison needed a clearer format

- pricing feedback was too detached from configuration choices

These findings directly shaped the redesign priorities.

blocks.title: Iteration and delivery details
blocks.content:
ITERATION AND DELIVERY DETAILS

The work went through several rounds of design exploration before reaching the integrated quotation flow.

I also prepared handoff specifications, responsive designs, and design QA follow-up for the outsourced development partner. The later phases extended the work to co-ownership flows, edge cases, and additional implementation details.
This project reinforced how closely discoverability and usability can be linked. Sometimes the right design answer is not to optimize one flow, but to solve the system around it first.
It also showed how important it is to reduce technical anxiety in high-intent journeys: users do not need every concept simplified, but they do need enough clarity to keep moving with confidence.

name: Financing Simulator — Reshape 2026
headline: Redesigning Renault and Dacia's financing simulator to improve comprehension, conversion, and modularity across markets.
roleSummary: Principal design owner: discovery, redesign, testing, accessibility, prototype creation, and stakeholder alignment across business, legal, and engineering.
summary: Redesigning Renault and Dacia's financing simulator to make financing easier to understand and act on, while navigating accessibility requirements, legal constraints, and multi-country complexity.
challenge: The financing simulator was useful once reached, but too hard to find, too rigid in its parameter model, and too weak at helping users move from simulation to action across a multi-country context.

blocks.content: Redesigning Renault and Dacia's financing simulator meant making financing easier to understand, easier to act on, and easier to trust while balancing accessibility, legal constraints, multi-country complexity, and modular product ambitions.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Make financing easier to understand
Reduce friction in key interactions
Improve conversion potential and next-step clarity
Raise accessibility standards on the product

blocks.quote: Product angle | The redesign aims to move the simulator from an isolated calculator to a clearer, more actionable, more accessible financing product embedded in the broader vehicle journey.

blocks.content: The simulator had four overlapping product risks.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Value risk: the tool gave users a monthly price, but not enough reassurance, clarity, or next steps to make the simulation truly useful.
Usability risk: several parts of the experience created friction, from parameter wording to service comprehension, offer readability, and action visibility.
Viability risk: the simulator was expected to contribute to conversion, but the experience did not yet fully support lead generation or modular reuse across the journey.
Feasibility risk: the redesign had to work across countries, legal constraints, brand-system silos, and multiple stakeholders with different priorities.

blocks.content: I was the principal owner of the design work on this project.
My contribution included:

blocks.title: Key points
items: running a discovery user test on the current simulator to identify the main user pain points
auditing our existing financing simulators across the ecosystem
benchmarking competitors
creating the strategic recommendation direction with input from data and validation from design leadership
designing improved versions of the simulator in desktop and mobile
creating responsive, multi-version interactive prototypes
defining and running a new validation test in A/B comparison between two layouts
improving accessibility on the design side and formulating implementation recommendations
collaborating with legal, countries, financial-services stakeholders, and the Renault site-owner team on placement and product evolution

blocks.title: Current experience audit
blocks.description: Show the current simulator annotated with the key pain points: discoverability, parameter clarity, price evolution, and CTA hierarchy.
blocks.caption: Visual placeholder

blocks.title: What I learned from the current product

blocks.content: The first discovery test made one thing clear: the problem was not that users did not see the value of financing, but that the current simulator was not helping them enough.
The main issues were:

blocks.title: Key points
items: discoverability was too weak on the current pages
some parameters and services were harder to understand than they should have been
action buttons were not prominent enough
users needed an easier way to follow price evolution while exploring options
the simulator did too little to turn a completed simulation into a useful next step

blocks.content: The redesign started from product friction, not from a visual refresh.

blocks.title: Workstream overview
blocks.description: Show the 3 workstreams together: accessibility, MVP and target vision, and user testing.
blocks.caption: Visual placeholder

blocks.content: I redesigned the simulator using more compact components to reduce friction and make the experience feel lighter and more readable.
I introduced sticky elements so price evolution remained visible while users modified financing options. This improved continuity and reduced the feeling of losing context while exploring scenarios.
I improved the presentation and readability of optional services so users could better understand what they were selecting and what was included.
I gave more visibility to key action buttons and tested wording variations to better support conversion.

A major evolution in the project was pushing the simulator toward a more modular role. This included ideas such as dedicated discovery paths, simulation receipt, stronger lead-generation logic, tighter integration at the end of configuration, and future dealer-locator integration to reduce friction in the pre-approval journey.
I structured the work into different ambition levels and built a responsive multi-version prototype close to reality to support testing and decision-making.

blocks.title: Tested layouts
blocks.description: Show the 2 tested directions side by side with the hypotheses behind each one.
blocks.caption: Visual placeholder

blocks.content: I used AI pragmatically to improve speed and fidelity where it made sense.
This included:

blocks.title: Key points
items: an AI agent I created to help generate the test protocol and test grid from our hypotheses
AI support for synthesizing findings after tests
prototype production supported by tools such as Figma Make and Claude Code to create a realistic, responsive, multi-version prototype

blocks.content: The goal was not to replace product thinking, but to move faster on execution-heavy tasks while preserving rigor in decision-making.
Accessibility was not treated as a side task.

Alongside the redesign, I worked on accessibility using a dedicated internal agent and created an audit restitution template to make collaboration with developers clearer and more actionable. I addressed accessibility issues on the design side and formulated recommendations for the implementation side, keeping WCAG constraints in mind throughout the work.

I also worked on multibrand design-system elements dedicated to this product, using the constructor site tokens despite structural silos between the Renault site-owner team and the financial-services team.

blocks.title: Accessibility audit extract
blocks.description: Show one real audit slice with issue, severity, recommendation, and implementation note.
blocks.caption: Visual placeholder

blocks.content: The new version is currently being validated through user testing, including an A/B test between two different layouts.

This validation phase is more complex because new stakeholders brought additional project history and constraints, which required revisiting parts of the prototype. That added complexity, but it also grounded the direction more strongly.

At the same time, I am working with the Renault site-owner team to improve access to the simulator through better CTA visibility and placement. This part remains politically sensitive and is still in progress.

blocks.quote: The redesign is not shipped yet, but the work has already reframed the simulator as a more modular, more accessible, and more conversion-oriented product rather than a standalone financing widget.

blocks.title: What this project is really about

blocks.content: This project is not only about making a calculator easier to use.
It is about making financing easier to understand, easier to act on, and easier to trust while navigating legal review, country constraints, site ownership, accessibility, and product politics.

blocks.title: Research and testing details
blocks.content:
RESEARCH, BENCHMARK, AND TESTING DETAILS

I ran a discovery user test on the current simulator, then a second user test on the redesigned version using an A/B setup across two layout directions.

I also completed a benchmark of competing financing tools and an audit of our current simulator landscape to identify recurring issues, opportunities, and constraints.

UserTesting was used for the research phase, and the findings helped define hypotheses, protocol, and design priorities.

blocks.title: Multi-country, legal, and stakeholder complexity
blocks.content:
MULTI-COUNTRY, LEGAL, AND STAKEHOLDER COMPLEXITY

A large part of the complexity came from constraints outside the interface itself.

The product had to work across countries, absorb legal requirements, and evolve through diplomatic alignment with multiple markets and internal teams. User testing became a useful lever to defend proposals and move conversations forward with countries, legal teams, and leadership.
This project reinforced how often the real work of product design happens at the intersection of usability, conversion, system constraints, and organizational politics.

It also showed how much leverage can come from combining research, prototyping, accessibility thinking, and AI-assisted execution when the product stakes are high and the stakeholder landscape is fragmented.
